summary: Brian Claire, founder of Ottawa's Blueprint Accounting, explains how he turned a Slack conversation into a working payroll-app prototype in about ten minutes using Claude and Cursor, then validated it with a survey of 50 to 60 accounting firms before paying an agency to build the real product. He walks through the twelve-month path from prototype to paying clients, the rebrand from Payday to Nooma after a trademark conflict with ADP, co-founder and shareholder-agreement lessons, and why he thinks the speed of AI development lets small teams compete with incumbents like Wagepoint.
takeaways: Brian built the first Payday prototype in about ten minutes: he had Claude summarize a Slack thread with his co-founder into a prompt, then handed that prompt to Cursor, and the only cost was token credits.

A survey of roughly 50 to 60 accounting firms found they juggle five to six payroll platforms on average, which is why the multi-client dashboard (the Hub) got more interest than the payroll engine itself.

The timeline from idea to paying clients was about six months: two months of prototype and conversations starting July 1, four months with an Australian agency working roughly 35 hours a week, and live by January.
Payday was rebranded to Nooma after merging with developer Hugh's Nooma Track, partly because ADP owns a trademark on the word Payday.

On partnerships Brian says to be aligned on vision, get your own lawyer rather than relying on the company's counsel, and understand exit terms like shotgun clauses and four-year vesting with a one-year cliff.

Nooma's stated goal is to automate more than 80 percent of payroll prep with a human still reviewing every run; Brian frames it as letting one payroll specialist handle ten times the clients rather than replacing people.

Brian's closing sticky note is 'discipline over motivation', and his standing advice for anyone learning AI is to tinker with the tools directly and build a reusable prompt library instead of only watching videos.
